profile.campus: Google Northern Virginia (Reston / Loudoun County / Prince William County), VA
profile.address: 13174 Sapphire Ridge Place, Amberleigh Station, Bristow, Prince William County, VA 20136
profile.reading:
This building is part of Google's Northern Virginia data center footprint, at 13174 Sapphire Ridge Place in the Amberleigh Station area of Bristow, Prince William County, per mapping data. Google's own Virginia locations page, fetched this session, does not name individual buildings within its Northern Virginia footprint, so this specific structure is not independently confirmed against a Google-published building index beyond its OSM-derived address.

Google's cloud infrastructure operates as a business of Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOGL/GOOG, SEC CIK 0001652044), headquartered at 1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, California. Google's own Virginia data center location page, fetched fresh this session, states the company established a Virginia presence in 2009, purchased Northern Virginia land in 2017, opened its first facility in 2019, expanded a second Loudoun County facility in 2021, and opened a third in Prince William County in 2023; in 2025 Google announced a $9 billion investment for 2025-2026 spanning existing Northern Virginia sites and a new Chesterfield County campus. Google reports $15.6 billion in Virginia economic activity and over 36,000 employee volunteer hours since 2010.

Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley corridor, of which this Bristow-area building is part, hosts large single-tenant campuses for AWS and Meta and colocation operators including Digital Realty and Equinix, all separately tracked in this registry, though Google's own public materials describe its Virginia footprint in aggregate rather than naming individual buildings or per-building capacity figures.

Loudoun and Prince William counties sit at the center of what industry trackers call Data Center Alley, the largest concentration of data center capacity in the world by aggregate power draw, a status Loudoun County's own economic development office has cited in public materials for over a decade. Dominion Energy, the regional utility, has repeatedly flagged this corridor in integrated resource plan filings with the Virginia State Corporation Commission as the single largest driver of new electricity demand in its Virginia service territory, prompting new transmission and generation investment. Virginia's data center sales-and-use tax exemption, administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership and renewed by the General Assembly, has been a material factor in Google and other hyperscalers continuing to expand in the corridor rather than building only in lower-tax states, though Google has not disclosed how much exemption value this specific facility has claimed.

reading.body:
This building at 13174 Sapphire Ridge Place in Bristow, Prince William County, is one structure within Google's Northern Virginia data center footprint, which Google describes in aggregate rather than per-building. Google does not publish a megawatt IT capacity figure for this individual building, so its direct contribution to AI compute cannot be measured from disclosed specifications. The building opened in 2023 as part of Google's third facility in the Northern Virginia corridor.

Northern Virginia, anchored by the Loudoun County corridor known as Data Center Alley, is the largest data center market in the world by capacity. This Bristow location sits in a region where Dominion Energy has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing load on its system, and where Google, AWS, Meta, and major colocation operators operate large single-tenant campuses. Virginia's sales-and-use tax exemption for data center equipment has been credited by local officials with accelerating expansion in this corridor.

Google announced a $9 billion investment spanning 2025 and 2026 across existing Northern Virginia sites and a new Chesterfield County campus, but does not disclose which portion applies to which individual building. This facility's significance lies in its location within a region now binding the growth of AI compute to power infrastructure and grid capacity rather than to building availability. The specific megawatt contribution of this Bristow building remains unpublished.
